en.title: Psychology: the whole course
en.short: What psychology is, how a psychology degree is organised, the main areas, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What psychology is
sections.text:
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behaviour. It asks how people perceive, learn, remember, think, feel, act and relate to others, and how biological, social and cultural processes shape those abilities. It is not simply common sense. Psychologists build theories, make predictions and test them with systematic observation, measurement and experiment.

The subject has several levels. Biological psychology studies the brain, hormones and genes. Cognitive psychology studies attention, memory, language and reasoning. Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan. Social psychology studies how people influence one another. Clinical and counselling psychology study mental health and helping. These levels often meet in one question.

Psychology also has competing schools, including structuralism, functionalism, behaviourism, psychoanalysis, Gestalt psychology, humanistic psychology and the cognitive approach. Modern psychology is plural: different approaches ask different questions and use different methods. Where they disagree, this course sets out each view and its evidence.

sections.heading: How a psychology degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc in psychology is commonly a four-year programme, and the final year usually includes a research project. In the UK, a BSc is usually three years full-time (four in Scotland), and an MSc one year full-time. In South Africa, a BSc is usually three years, often followed by an honours year (a one-year postgraduate qualification) and then a master’s for professional training. These are common patterns only. Check your own handbook and the current rules of your country’s regulator.

A degree usually starts with foundations and methods, then moves to core areas, then to advanced options and a project. A master’s degree goes deeper into theory and methods and ends with a dissertation. A degree does not by itself make you a licensed practitioner. Registration rules differ by country, so check the current official requirements.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics come first: psychology as a science and its history and schools; research methods; statistics; biological bases of behaviour; sensation and perception; learning; memory; cognition, language and thought; motivation and emotion; and lifespan development foundations. These give the vocabulary and methods for later work. The order moves from foundations to applications, so each later topic can use earlier ideas.

Core topics deepen them: cognitive psychology; child and adolescent development; social psychology; personality and individual differences; abnormal psychology and mental health; clinical psychology; counselling psychology; industrial and organisational psychology; educational psychology; health psychology; psychometrics, including test reliability (consistency) and validity (whether a test measures what it claims); research methods in psychology; ethics and professional practice; cross-cultural and African psychology; and the psychology research project. The project brings methods, ethics and writing together.

At master’s level, advanced cognitive neuroscience, advanced social psychology and advanced research methods and statistics deepen specialist knowledge. The dissertation trains you to design, conduct and report an independent study.

sections.heading: How to study psychology
sections.text:
Study actively. Read a section, close the book and explain it in your own words. Then test yourself with questions. Space your practice over days and weeks; cramming feels productive but fades quickly. Use concrete examples, including cases set in your own society, and ask whether a finding would hold in another culture.

Learn methods and statistics early and keep using them. When you read a study, ask what was measured, how, in whom, and with what result. Learn to read a table and a simple test statistic. Write regularly, in short paragraphs with a clear claim and evidence. For clinical, counselling and ethical topics, learn the limits of your training. Do not diagnose yourself or others.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
The most common mistake is to treat psychology as common sense. Another is to confuse correlation with causation: two things can move together without one causing the other. Students also overgeneralise from a single study, or from samples drawn only from Western universities, and ignore base rates, meaning how common something is in a population, when judging risk.

In statistics, students report a result without saying how large the effect is, or use a test without checking its assumptions. In essays, they describe a theory but do not evaluate it. In practice topics, they forget consent, confidentiality and competence. Finally, many students ignore the rules on plagiarism and citation. Keep a record of every source you use, and check your institution’s rules.

keyPoints: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour, not a collection of common-sense sayings.
A degree normally moves from foundations and methods to core areas and then to a project or dissertation.
Learn research methods and statistics early; they are the tools for judging every claim.
Correlation does not prove causation, and one study rarely settles a question.
Check your own country’s and institution’s rules on degree length, awards and professional practice.
Ethical practice and cultural context are part of psychology, not optional extras.

en.title: Psychology as a Science: History and Schools of Thought
en.short: What psychology is, its goals, scientific attitude, key debates and main schools from Wundt to cognitive psychology.

sections.heading: Psychology and its goals
sections.text: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour. Its goals are description (what happens), explanation (why it happens), prediction (what is likely next) and change (influencing behaviour or improving wellbeing). Psychology uses evidence rather than intuition alone. It also asks how reliable and valid its evidence is.

sections.heading: Science and debates
sections.text: The scientific attitude means curiosity, scepticism and openness to evidence. Claims must be testable and open to replication. A theory that cannot be tested is not scientific. Two long debates are nature versus nurture, whether biology or environment shapes behaviour, and determinism versus free will, whether actions are caused or chosen. Many psychologists treat nature and nurture as interacting, and some adopt compatibilism, the view that causes and choice can coexist.

sections.heading: Historical schools
sections.text: Modern psychology is often dated from Wilhelm Wundt’s experimental laboratory in Leipzig, Germany, in 1879. Early experimental psychology studied conscious experience through introspection, the careful reporting of inner experience. Behaviourism, associated with John B. Watson and B. F. Skinner, rejected introspection and studied observable behaviour and learning. Gestalt psychology (from a German word for form or whole) argued that perception and thought are organised wholes, not separate parts. Psychoanalysis, from Sigmund Freud, emphasised unconscious conflict and early experience. Humanistic psychology, with Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow, stressed growth, choice and subjective meaning. Cognitive psychology studies mental processes such as attention and memory, often using the computer as a model.

sections.heading: Comparing assumptions
sections.text: These schools differ in assumptions. Behaviourism looks to environment and observable responses; psychoanalysis to hidden conflict; humanistic psychology to choice and growth; cognitive psychology to internal processing; Gestalt to whole patterns. For example, a Nigerian student named Amina avoids exams. A behaviourist may explain this as learned avoidance, a cognitive psychologist as fearful thoughts, and a humanistic psychologist as blocked confidence. Each view can be tested in its own way. No single school explains everything.

keyPoints: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behaviour.
Its goals are description, explanation, prediction and change.
The scientific attitude requires testable claims, scepticism and openness to evidence.
Nature and nurture, and determinism and free will, are usually treated as interacting rather than simple opposites.
Wundt’s 1879 laboratory is a common starting point for experimental psychology.
Behaviourism, Gestalt, psychoanalysis, humanistic and cognitive psychology differ in what they study and assume.

en.title: Introduction to Research Methods in Psychology
en.short: Variables, hypotheses, sampling, research designs, reliability, validity, bias and ethics in psychology research.

sections.heading: Variables and hypotheses
sections.text: Psychologists study variables, which are qualities or quantities that can differ, such as sleep, anxiety or test score. An operational definition states exactly how a variable will be measured or manipulated, for example sleep loss as sleeping fewer than five hours in a laboratory night. This makes it possible for other researchers to repeat the study. A hypothesis is a testable prediction about a relationship between variables. In an experiment, the independent variable is manipulated and the dependent variable is measured.

sections.heading: Sampling
sections.text: A population is the whole group of interest; a sample is the part studied. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection and improves representativeness. Convenience sampling uses whoever is available and is common in student projects, but it can produce sampling bias. Sample size affects precision, but a large biased sample is still biased. Researchers should describe how participants were selected.

sections.heading: Designs
sections.text: Experimental designs manipulate an independent variable and use random assignment, placing participants in conditions by chance; only these can support causal claims. Quasi-experimental designs compare groups that are not randomly assigned, such as students who chose different courses. Correlational designs measure two variables without manipulation and show association, not causation. Surveys collect self-report data from many people. Case studies examine one person or a small group in depth. For example, comparing volunteers who join a study group with those who do not is quasi-experimental, not experimental.

sections.heading: Quality and ethics
sections.text: Reliability is consistency: a measure gives similar results on repeated use. Validity is whether a measure or study measures what it claims. Bias is a systematic error, such as leading questions, cues that tell participants what is expected, or experimenter expectations. Ethical rules usually include informed consent, agreeing freely after understanding the study, right to withdraw, confidentiality, minimising harm, and explaining the study afterwards when deception was used. Deception must be justified and approved. Rules differ by country and institution, so check the local code and ethics committee.

keyPoints: A variable is anything that can take different values; an operational definition says how it is measured.
A hypothesis is a testable prediction about a relationship between variables.
Random sampling reduces sampling bias; convenience sampling often does not.
Experiments use manipulation and random assignment and can support causal claims.
Quasi-experiments, correlational studies, surveys and case studies cannot by themselves establish causation.
Reliability is consistency, validity is accuracy, and ethical research needs consent, safety and approval.

en.title: Statistics for Psychology
en.short: This summary covers describing data, the normal curve, z-scores, correlation and null hypothesis tests.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Levels of measurement set what arithmetic is allowed. Nominal data are labels, such as diagnosis. Ordinal data are ranked but gaps are unequal. Interval data have equal gaps but no true zero, such as temperature in °C. Ratio data have equal gaps and a true zero, such as reaction time.

A frequency distribution counts how often each value occurs. Use bar charts for categories and histograms for continuous scores. Central tendency gives a typical score: mean, median and mode. Variability gives spread: range, variance and standard deviation (SD), the typical distance from the mean.

sections.heading: Normal curve and z-scores
sections.text:
The normal curve is a symmetric bell-shaped distribution. A z-score says how many SDs a score lies from the mean: z = (X − μ) ÷ σ.

If mean = 60 and SD = 10, a score of 75 gives z = (75 − 60) ÷ 10 = 1.5, so it is 1.5 SD above the mean. About 68% lies within 1 SD, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.

sections.heading: Correlation and sampling
sections.text:
Correlation measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship. Pearson’s r runs from −1 to +1; 0 means no linear relationship. Correlation does not prove causation.

A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic across repeated samples. Its spread is the standard error, which shrinks as sample size grows.

sections.heading: Null hypothesis tests
sections.text:
Null hypothesis testing starts with H0, usually no effect. The alternative denies this. A test statistic gives a p-value: the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if H0 is true. It is not the probability that H0 is true.

Alpha is set before the test; if p is below alpha, reject H0. A Type I error rejects a true H0 (false positive). A Type II error fails to reject a false H0 (false negative). t-tests compare means: t = (mean difference) ÷ standard error. Chi-square compares observed O with expected E: chi-square = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E).

keyPoints: Levels of measurement are nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio; they limit which statistics are valid.
The mean, median and mode summarise central tendency, while range, variance and standard deviation summarise variability.
A z-score is z = (X − μ) ÷ σ, the number of standard deviations a score lies from the mean.
Correlation r runs from −1 to +1 and measures linear association, not causation.
A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if H0 is true, not the probability that H0 is true.
Type I error rejects a true H0; Type II error fails to reject a false H0; t = (mean difference) ÷ standard error and chi-square = Σ((O − E)² ÷ E).

en.title: Biological Bases of Behaviour
en.short: Neurons, action potentials, synapses, nervous system, brain, hormones, genes and methods.

sections.heading: Neuron and action potential
sections.text: Neurons receive, integrate and send information. A neuron has dendrites, which receive signals; a cell body with the nucleus; and an axon, which carries impulses away. Myelin, a fatty sheath, speeds conduction. At rest the inside is negative relative to the outside, often around −70 mV. If a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium ions rush in and the membrane briefly reverses. This is the action potential, an all-or-none electrical signal along the axon.

sections.heading: Synapse and neurotransmitters
sections.text: At a synapse, the junction between neurons, an axon terminal releases neurotransmitters, chemicals stored in vesicles. They cross the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the next cell, exciting or inhibiting it. Neurotransmitters are then broken down or taken back up, ending the signal. Examples include acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid). Drugs and diseases can change these steps, for example by blocking receptors or altering reuptake.

sections.heading: Nervous system and brain
sections.text: The nervous system has two main divisions. The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system links it to the body and divides into the somatic system, for voluntary movement and sensation, and the autonomic system, for involuntary functions. The autonomic system has sympathetic and parasympathetic branches. Key brain structures include the brainstem, cerebellum, hypothalamus, limbic system (amygdala and hippocampus) and cerebral cortex, divided into frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes.

sections.heading: Hormones, genes and methods
sections.text: The endocrine system uses hormones, chemicals released by glands into the blood, to regulate growth, stress, metabolism and reproduction. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland. Genes influence behaviour through inherited tendencies and interactions with environment; twin and adoption studies estimate heritability, the share of group variation linked to genetic differences. Methods include lesion studies, electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials, and neuroimaging such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and positron emission tomography (PET). Case: Ngozi, a student, has a head injury and shows memory problems; tests and imaging help locate the affected area, though findings are probabilistic.

keyPoints: Neurons receive, integrate and transmit information; dendrites receive signals and axons conduct impulses.
An action potential is an all-or-none electrical signal triggered when the membrane reaches threshold.
Synaptic transmission converts an electrical signal into a chemical one and back again.
The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system links it to the body.
The endocrine system releases hormones into the blood, and genes interact with environment to influence behaviour.
Brain and behaviour are studied with lesions, EEG and neuroimaging, but findings are probabilistic.

en.title: Sensation and Perception: From Sense Organs to Meaning
en.short: How sense organs transduce stimuli, and how attention and the brain build perception.

sections.heading: Transduction and thresholds
sections.text:
Sensation begins when a sense organ detects physical energy and sensory receptors convert it into neural impulses. This conversion is sensory transduction.

The absolute threshold is the weakest stimulus a person can detect reliably. The difference threshold, or just noticeable difference, is the smallest change detected. Weber’s law says the difference threshold is a constant fraction of the original stimulus, though the fraction varies by sense. Sensory adaptation is reduced sensitivity after constant stimulation, such as a watch feeling less noticeable after a while.

sections.heading: Vision and hearing
sections.text:
In vision, light passes the cornea and lens, which focus it on the retina. Rods work in dim light and cones give colour and detail. Retinal cells send signals through the optic nerve.

In hearing, sound waves enter the pinna (outer ear) and ear canal, vibrate the eardrum, and move three small bones in the middle ear. The cochlea turns these vibrations into nerve signals from hair cells. The auditory nerve carries them to the brain.

sections.heading: Attention and organisation
sections.text:
Attention selects some information for deeper processing. Bottom-up processing starts from sensory features; top-down processing uses knowledge, expectations and context.

Gestalt psychologists showed that we group features by proximity, similarity, continuity and closure. A concrete case: Amina hears her name across a noisy market even though she was not listening to that speaker (the cocktail party effect), which shows that some unattended sound is still processed. She still groups stalls by colour and nearness.

sections.heading: Depth, constancy, illusions
sections.text:
Depth cues include binocular disparity (each eye sees a slightly different image) and convergence (the eyes turn inward for near objects), and monocular cues such as overlap, relative size, linear perspective and motion parallax.

Perceptual constancy keeps objects looking stable in size, shape and colour despite changing retinal images. Illusions such as the Müller-Lyer lines and the Ponzo illusion show that perception is an active construction, not a direct copy.

keyPoints: Sensory transduction converts stimulus energy into neural signals.
The absolute threshold is the weakest reliably detected stimulus; the difference threshold is the smallest detectable change.
Sensory adaptation reduces sensitivity to a constant stimulus.
Vision uses rods and cones in the retina; hearing uses hair cells in the cochlea.
Bottom-up processing starts with sensory features, while top-down processing uses knowledge and expectations.
Gestalt grouping, depth cues and perceptual constancy show that perception is an active construction.

en.title: Learning: Conditioning and Behaviour Change
en.short: Covers habituation, classical and operant conditioning, observational learning, reinforcement schedules and behaviour change.

sections.heading: Habituation and classical conditioning
sections.text: Habituation is a decline in response to a repeated harmless stimulus. A student stops noticing a ticking clock. Classical conditioning is learning by association. In Pavlov’s dog studies, food is an unconditioned stimulus (US) that naturally causes salivation, an unconditioned response (UR). A bell paired repeatedly with food becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS), and the bell alone causes a conditioned response (CR). Acquisition is the learning phase; extinction is the weakening when the CS is presented without the US; spontaneous recovery is the return of the CR after a pause.

sections.heading: Operant conditioning
sections.text: Operant conditioning is learning from consequences. A behaviour followed by reinforcement becomes more likely; a behaviour followed by punishment becomes less likely. Positive means adding a stimulus and negative means removing one. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant, such as praise. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, such as taking a painkiller to end a headache, and also strengthens behaviour. Negative reinforcement is not punishment. Punishment weakens behaviour, either by adding an unpleasant stimulus or removing a pleasant one.

sections.heading: Schedules and observational learning
sections.text: Schedules of reinforcement describe when rewards follow behaviour. Continuous reinforcement rewards every response and is useful for starting a habit. Partial schedules are fixed ratio (after a set number of responses), variable ratio (after an unpredictable number), fixed interval (after a set time) and variable interval (after an unpredictable time). Variable schedules usually produce steady, persistent responding. Observational learning, studied by Albert Bandura, is learning by watching models. It depends on attention, retention, reproduction and motivation.

sections.heading: Application and case
sections.text: Application: to change behaviour, define the target, choose reinforcement or punishment, and monitor effects. A case: Amina wants to stop checking her phone while studying. She keeps the phone in a drawer for 25 minutes and then takes a short break. The break reinforces study; removing the phone reduces cues. Her brother watches her routine and copies it, showing observational learning. During extinction the behaviour may briefly increase or return after a pause, so consistency matters.

keyPoints: Habituation is a reduced response to a repeated harmless stimulus.
Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus until the neutral stimulus alone elicits a response.
Reinforcement increases behaviour; punishment decreases it, and negative reinforcement is not punishment.
Continuous reinforcement is best for starting a behaviour; variable schedules make behaviour persistent.
Observational learning requires attention, retention, reproduction and motivation.
Behaviour change works best when the target behaviour, reinforcement or punishment, and results are monitored.

en.title: Memory: Encoding, Storage and Retrieval
en.short: How memory encodes, stores and retrieves information, and how to study it effectively.

sections.heading: Encoding, storage, retrieval
sections.text: Memory has three basic operations. Encoding turns information into a form the brain can keep. Storage maintains it over time. Retrieval brings it back when needed. Encoding is stronger when material is processed for meaning rather than only repeated. Storage is not a single store: sensory memory holds raw impressions for under a second or a few seconds; working memory holds a small amount for seconds while it is used; long-term memory can keep information for years.

sections.heading: Memory systems
sections.text: Sensory memory includes iconic (visual) and echoic (sound) traces. Working memory is a limited workspace for holding and manipulating information, often described by Baddeley and Hitch as separate components. Long-term memory divides into explicit and implicit. Explicit memory is conscious recall: episodic memory for events and semantic memory for facts. Implicit memory affects behaviour without conscious recall, such as skills and priming. Example: after learning to ride a bicycle, a student may not remember the first lesson but still steer automatically.

sections.heading: Forgetting and reconstruction
sections.text: Forgetting can come from decay, retrieval failure, or interference. Proactive interference means old learning disrupts new learning; retroactive interference means new learning disrupts old. Memory is also reconstructive: people fill gaps using expectations and later information. In eyewitness cases, misleading questions can alter reports, a misinformation effect studied by Elizabeth Loftus. A witness who hears “the tall thief” may later remember height inaccurately. Confidence is not a reliable sign of accuracy.

sections.heading: Evidence-based study
sections.text: Two strong strategies are retrieval practice and spaced practice. Retrieval practice means testing yourself instead of only rereading. Spaced practice means spreading study over days rather than cramming. Interleaving related topics can also help. A student like Chidi prepares for a psychology test by writing questions from each chapter, answering them without notes, and revisiting wrong answers after two days. This uses retrieval and spacing together.

keyPoints: Encoding, storage and retrieval are the three basic memory operations.
Sensory memory is brief; working memory is limited; long-term memory is relatively enduring.
Explicit memory is conscious, including episodic and semantic memory; implicit memory is unconscious, including skills and priming.
Interference and reconstruction explain many forgetting and eyewitness errors.
Retrieval practice and spaced practice are better supported than rereading alone.

en.title: Cognition, Language and Thought
en.short: Attention, concepts, problem solving, reasoning, heuristics, biases, and language structure and acquisition.

sections.heading: Attention and concepts
sections.text:
Attention selects some information for deeper processing. Selective attention focuses on one source and ignores others; divided attention shares effort between tasks, at a cost in speed or accuracy.

A concept is a mental category that treats different things as equivalent. Categories may be represented by defining features, by a prototype (the best example), or by stored exemplars. A penguin is a bird, but a sparrow is closer to most people’s bird prototype.

sections.heading: Problem solving and reasoning
sections.text:
Problem solving uses algorithms, step-by-step procedures that guarantee a solution, or heuristics, quick rules of thumb that may fail. Means-end analysis reduces the gap between current state and goal. Functional fixedness is failure to see a new use for a familiar object.

Deductive reasoning draws a conclusion that must follow from the premises: All mammals are warm-blooded; whales are mammals; therefore whales are warm-blooded. Inductive reasoning generalises from cases to a probable conclusion, but never guarantees it.

sections.heading: Judgement and decision making
sections.text:
People often judge with heuristics. The availability heuristic estimates frequency by how easily examples come to mind. The representativeness heuristic judges probability by similarity to a prototype and can ignore base rates (how common something is). Anchoring and adjustment starts from an initial value and adjusts too little.

Biases include confirmation bias, seeking evidence that supports a belief, and framing, where the same choice described as a gain or a loss changes preference. After hearing of a plane crash, a traveller may overestimate the danger of flying because crashes are easy to recall.

sections.heading: Language
sections.text:
Language has structure: phonemes are the smallest sound units, morphemes the smallest meaning units, syntax the rules for combining words, semantics meaning, and pragmatics meaning in context.

Acquisition is explained by behaviourist learning (imitation and reinforcement), by Chomsky’s nativist view of an innate capacity, and by interactionist views that add social input. The critical period hypothesis holds that first language is best acquired in childhood; evidence is debated. Linguistic relativity suggests language may shape thought; the strong version is not supported.

keyPoints: Attention can be selective or divided; dividing attention usually costs speed or accuracy.
Concepts and categories can be represented by defining features, prototypes or exemplars.
Algorithms guarantee a solution when correctly applied; heuristics are faster but fallible.
Deductive reasoning yields conclusions that must follow; inductive reasoning yields probable conclusions.
Availability, representativeness and anchoring are common judgement heuristics, and confirmation bias and framing are common biases.
Language is structured at the levels of phonemes, morphemes, syntax, semantics and pragmatics; acquisition is explained by behaviourist, nativist and interactionist accounts.

en.title: Motivation and Emotion
en.short: Covers drive, arousal, incentive and humanistic motivation, plus emotion theories, appraisal and culture.

sections.heading: Motivation theories
sections.text:
Motivation starts, directs and sustains behaviour. Drive-reduction theory (Clark Hull) says a biological need creates tension, a drive, and behaviour that reduces it is reinforced; the body seeks a balanced internal state, homeostasis.

Arousal theory says people seek an optimal level of arousal. The Yerkes-Dodson law says moderate arousal often suits complex tasks, while simple tasks may tolerate more. Incentive theory stresses external pulls such as rewards. Humanistic theory, especially Maslow’s hierarchy, says needs range from physiological and safety needs to belonging, esteem and self-actualisation, the full use of potential. The theories complement one another.

sections.heading: Intrinsic, achievement, eating
sections.text:
Intrinsic motivation comes from interest or enjoyment in the activity. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside rewards or pressures. Rewards can sometimes weaken intrinsic interest, depending on how they are used.

Achievement motivation is the need to meet high standards and avoid failure; it predicts persistence on challenging tasks. Eating behaviour is shaped by hunger and satiety signals, learning, mood, portion size and culture. Chidi eats more at a party after a meal because social cues and tasty food pull him, not because his body needs energy.

sections.heading: Emotion theories
sections.text:
Emotion is a brief response involving feeling, arousal, expression and action. James-Lange theory says bodily changes come first and we feel them as emotion. Cannon-Bard theory says arousal and feeling happen together.

Schachter-Singer two-factor theory says arousal plus a cognitive label produces emotion. Appraisal theories, such as Lazarus’s, stress how we evaluate an event as relevant to our goals; primary appraisal asks if it matters, secondary appraisal asks if we can cope.

sections.heading: Expression and culture
sections.text:
Facial expressions communicate emotion. Some researchers, notably Ekman, argue that certain basic emotions have recognisable universal expressions, but the evidence is debated.

Culture sets display rules, which are norms about when and how to show emotion. Culture also shapes what events trigger emotions and how people describe them, so experience and display vary across societies.

keyPoints: Drive-reduction theory links needs to tension and homeostasis.
Arousal theory and the Yerkes-Dodson law relate performance to optimal arousal.
Incentive theory stresses external pulls; humanistic theory stresses growth and self-actualisation.
Intrinsic motivation comes from interest, extrinsic from external rewards or pressures.
James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and Schachter-Singer differ on the order of body, thought and feeling.
Display rules are cultural norms about showing emotion, and universality of facial expressions is debated.

en.title: Lifespan Development: Foundations
en.short: Physical, cognitive and social development across life, with Piaget, Vygotsky, Erikson and attachment.

sections.heading: Lifespan perspective
sections.text: Lifespan development studies how people change and stay the same from conception to death. It covers physical growth, cognitive abilities, and social and emotional relationships. Development is lifelong, multidimensional and shaped by context, so no single stage is isolated. Prenatal life is affected by maternal health and teratogens, meaning substances or conditions that harm the embryo or foetus. Childhood brings rapid motor and language gains; adolescence brings puberty and growing independence; adulthood and ageing bring role changes and gradual physical change.

sections.heading: Theories
sections.text: Jean Piaget proposed that children pass through stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational. He argued that children build schemas, mental frameworks, through assimilation, fitting new information into existing schemas, and accommodation, changing schemas when new information does not fit. Lev Vygotsky stressed social interaction and the zone of proximal development, the gap between what a learner can do alone and with help. Erik Erikson described eight psychosocial stages, each with a crisis such as trust versus mistrust in infancy. Attachment theory, developed by John Bowlby and tested by Mary Ainsworth, holds that early caregiver bonds shape later relationships.

sections.heading: Concrete case
sections.text: Consider Ada, aged four, who says a tall narrow glass holds more water than a short wide one. By about seven or eight, most children say the amount is the same if nothing is added or removed. This is conservation. Piaget used such tasks to study preoperational and concrete operational thinking. Vygotsky would ask how an adult’s prompts or a peer’s explanation help Ada solve the task. The case shows that cognitive change depends on both maturation and social support.

sections.heading: Nature and nurture
sections.text: The nature-nurture debate asks how much development comes from genes and how much from environment. Most psychologists now reject a simple split. Genes and environments interact: a child’s temperament may evoke different care, and poverty or schooling can change opportunities. Development is also probabilistic, not fixed. Cross-cultural research reminds us that norms for independence, parenting and ageing vary, so findings from one country need checking elsewhere.

keyPoints: Development is lifelong and shaped by biological, psychological and social contexts.
Piaget proposed stage-like changes in thinking, from sensorimotor to formal operational.
Vygotsky emphasised social interaction, language and the zone of proximal development.
Erikson described eight psychosocial crises across the lifespan.
Attachment theory links early caregiver bonds to later relationships.
Nature and nurture interact, so development is not fixed by genes or environment alone.

en.title: Cognitive Psychology: Attention, Memory and Thinking
en.short: Theories and evidence on attention, working memory, long-term memory, language, reasoning and decision making.

sections.heading: Attention and capacity
sections.text:
Attention selects information for further processing. Early-selection models, such as Broadbent’s filter, block unattended input before meaning is extracted; late-selection models allow some unattended words to be processed. Load theory says perceptual load decides whether distractors are processed. Key paradigms include dichotic listening, the Stroop task and visual search. Capacity limits appear as dual-task interference.

Case: Amina studies in a busy Lagos market; her name spoken nearby captures attention, the cocktail-party effect, but reading a dense paragraph while holding a phone conversation slows both tasks.

sections.heading: Working memory
sections.text:
Working memory is a limited system for holding and manipulating information during tasks. Baddeley and Hitch proposed the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad and central executive; the episodic buffer was added later. Complex span tasks, such as reading span, predict comprehension and reasoning better than simple span. Capacity is debated: discrete slots versus shared resources.

Example: solving 17 × 24 while remembering a short list is harder than doing either alone, because both tasks compete for executive attention.

sections.heading: Long-term memory and language
sections.text:
Long-term memory divides into explicit memory (episodic and semantic) and implicit memory (procedural and priming). Forgetting can arise from failures in encoding, consolidation or retrieval, and retrieval cues strongly affect recall. Language processing is incremental: listeners integrate syntax and meaning as speech unfolds, and garden-path sentences show reanalysis. Models include spreading activation and connectionist networks.

The modularity debate asks whether language is an encapsulated module, as Fodor argued for input systems, or an interactive process.

sections.heading: Reasoning and rationality
sections.text:
Reasoning research contrasts normative logic with actual performance. The Wason selection task shows that content and context affect conditional reasoning. Judgement uses heuristics such as availability and representativeness, which can produce biases, as Tversky and Kahneman showed. Dual-process theories distinguish fast, intuitive System 1 from slow, deliberate System 2. Gigerenzer argues that heuristics can be ecologically rational.

The debate is whether people are irrational or rational within their environments. Decision making also involves framing and loss aversion.

keyPoints: Attention selects information, and its limits appear as dual-task interference.
Working memory holds and manipulates information, and complex span predicts higher cognition.
Long-term memory is explicit or implicit, and retrieval cues affect recall.
Language processing is incremental, and whether it is modular or interactive remains debated.
Heuristics are efficient but can cause biases, and dual-process theories describe fast and slow thinking.
Rationality depends on context, and ecological rationality asks whether heuristics fit the environment.

en.title: Child and Adolescent Development
en.short: Perceptual, cognitive, language, moral, social and emotional development, with research designs and resilience.

sections.heading: Studying change
sections.text: Developmental psychology studies change from infancy to adolescence. Cross-sectional designs compare ages at one time but confuse age with cohort, a group’s shared historical experience. Longitudinal designs follow the same people and show individual change, though they are slow and lose participants. Sequential designs combine both. Experiments test causes when random assignment is ethical; observation and interviews describe everyday behaviour. Correlation alone does not prove cause.

sections.heading: Perception, cognition, language
sections.text: Infants perceive contrasts and faces early, and perception sharpens with experience. Piaget described stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational. Later research shows some abilities appear earlier and development is often gradual. Vygotsky stressed guided participation and the zone of proximal development, the gap between what a child can do alone and with help. Language moves from cooing and babbling to words, grammar and pragmatics, the social use of language. Bilingual children may mix languages temporarily without confusion.

sections.heading: Moral and social
sections.text: Moral development moves from external rules to flexible judgement. Kohlberg proposed levels from punishment avoidance to principled reasoning; Gilligan argued care and relationships matter as much as justice. Social and emotional development includes emotion regulation, empathy and friendship. Parenting styles are authoritative, authoritarian, permissive and uninvolved; authoritative parenting, warm but firm, is linked with better adjustment in many studies, though culture shapes this. Peers provide practice in cooperation and conflict. Chidi, 13, joins a debate club; supportive peers and a warm parent help him manage exam anxiety.

sections.heading: Attachment and identity
sections.text: Attachment is the emotional bond between infant and caregiver. Bowlby argued it is biologically based; Ainsworth’s Strange Situation classified secure, insecure-avoidant and insecure-resistant patterns, and later work added disorganised. Secure attachment predicts better social confidence, not perfect outcomes. Erikson described identity versus role confusion; Marcia added statuses: diffusion, foreclosure, moratorium and achievement. Risk factors raise the chance of poor outcomes; protective factors and resilience, the capacity to adapt under stress, can offset them. Development is probabilistic, not fixed.

keyPoints: Cross-sectional designs compare ages, longitudinal designs follow the same people, and sequential designs combine both.
Piaget described stage-like cognitive change, while Vygotsky stressed guided participation and the zone of proximal development.
Language develops from early sounds to grammar and pragmatics, the social use of language.
Kohlberg emphasised justice reasoning and Gilligan emphasised care in moral development.
Secure attachment and authoritative parenting are linked with better adjustment, though culture and context matter.
Identity work in adolescence involves exploration and commitment, and resilience depends on protective factors offsetting risk.

en.title: Social Psychology: Situations, Groups and Culture
en.short: Social cognition, attribution, attitudes, persuasion, conformity, obedience, groups, prejudice, helping and close ties.

sections.heading: Thinking about people
sections.text: Social cognition is how people notice, store and use information about others. Attribution is the process of explaining behaviour. The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overrate personality and underrate situation when judging others. It appears in many cultures but tends to be stronger in individualistic settings. Attitudes are evaluations of people, objects or ideas. The elaboration likelihood model says persuasion works by a central route, when people think carefully about arguments, or a peripheral route, when they rely on cues such as source attractiveness. For example, a student sees a classmate arrive late and assumes laziness, though a transport strike caused it.

sections.heading: Influence and groups
sections.text: Conformity is changing behaviour to match group norms. Asch’s line-judgement studies showed that many people agree with an obviously wrong majority at least sometimes. Obedience is following an authority’s instruction. Milgram’s experiments showed that ordinary people may continue under situational pressure, though the ethics and cross-cultural reach of the findings are debated. Group processes include social loafing, where people put in less effort when responsibility is shared; groupthink, where cohesion suppresses dissent; and deindividuation, where crowd membership reduces self-awareness. These effects depend on task, culture and whether behaviour is visible.

sections.heading: Prejudice, harm and connection
sections.text: Prejudice is a negative attitude towards a group; discrimination is unfair behaviour, and stereotypes are generalised beliefs. Social identity (self-image drawn from group membership), competition and learning contribute. Aggression is behaviour intended to harm. It has biological and situational causes, and cultural norms shape when it is shown. Prosocial behaviour is helping. The bystander effect is the finding that people are less likely to help when many witnesses are present, partly through diffusion of responsibility, where each person feels less accountable. Close relationships rest on attachment, reciprocity (mutual give and take) and self-disclosure, with cultural norms shaping expectations. In a crowded market, a man collapses. If one bystander points to a specific person and says 'You, call for help', action becomes more likely.

keyPoints: Social psychology studies how situations, groups and culture shape thought and behaviour.
The fundamental attribution error overrates personality and underrates situation.
Persuasion can follow a central route of argument or a peripheral route of cues.
Conformity and obedience show that group and authority pressure can override personal judgement.
Prejudice is a negative attitude, distinct from stereotypes (beliefs) and discrimination (behaviour), and it arises from identity, competition and learning.
Helping falls with the bystander effect, while close relationships depend on attachment, reciprocity and self-disclosure.

en.title: Personality and Individual Differences
en.short: Trait, psychodynamic, humanistic, social-cognitive and biological views, stability, assessment and measurement quality.

sections.heading: Five approaches
sections.text: Trait approaches describe personality as stable dimensions on which people differ, such as the Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. They compare people by scores. Psychodynamic approaches, from Freud, stress unconscious conflict and early relationships, but many claims are hard to test. Humanistic approaches, such as Rogers and Maslow, focus on self-concept, growth and self-actualisation, the drive to fulfil potential. Social-cognitive approaches, such as Bandura’s, emphasise learning, expectancies and reciprocal determinism: person, behaviour and environment influence one another. Biological approaches study temperament, genetics and brain systems. Each approach answers different questions, and evidence is strongest where claims can be measured.

sections.heading: Stability and change
sections.text: Personality shows both consistency and change. Rank-order stability means people keep similar positions relative to others; it rises with age. Mean-level change means average scores shift, often with maturity. The person-situation debate asks whether behaviour is controlled by traits or situations. Most researchers now accept interaction: traits predict average tendencies, while situations shape particular acts. Cross-cultural work suggests the Big Five appear in many languages, but their meaning and measurement need care.

sections.heading: Assessing personality
sections.text: Assessment methods include self-report inventories, observer ratings, interviews, behavioural observation and projective tests. Self-reports are efficient but can be biased by self-presentation. Observer ratings add another view. Projective tests, such as the Rorschach, show weaker reliability and validity evidence than structured inventories. Reliability is consistency: test-retest, inter-rater and internal. Validity is whether a measure assesses what it claims: content, construct and criterion validity. A test can be reliable but invalid.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Suppose Amina scores high on conscientiousness on a questionnaire, and her supervisor rates her similarly. The agreement supports reliability. If the score also predicts her meeting deadlines, that supports criterion validity. It does not prove her personality is fixed; her behaviour may vary across settings.

keyPoints: Trait, psychodynamic, humanistic, social-cognitive and biological approaches make different assumptions and use different evidence.
Traits predict average behaviour better than single acts; person and situation interact.
Personality is both stable in rank order and capable of mean-level change across life.
Reliability concerns consistency; validity concerns whether a measure assesses the intended construct.
Self-report inventories are efficient but need observer or behavioural evidence where possible.
Projective tests generally have weaker reliability and validity evidence than structured inventories.

en.title: Abnormal Psychology and Mental Health
en.short: Definitions of abnormality, ICD and DSM classification, causes, stigma and culture.

sections.heading: Defining abnormality
sections.text: Abnormality has no single definition. Common criteria are statistical rarity, violation of social norms, personal distress and inability to function. Each is limited: rare talents are not disorders, norms change, and some disorders cause little distress. A mental disorder is better seen as a clinically significant pattern of distress or impairment, not simply oddness. Culture and context shape what counts as a symptom.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.text: Classification systems provide shared criteria. The ICD is published by WHO; the DSM by the American Psychiatric Association. Common current editions are ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR, but editions, codes and legal criteria vary by country and year, so check the official current source. Categories improve communication and research but can create false borders. Reliability means agreement between clinicians; validity means the category captures a real condition. Major groups include anxiety, mood, psychotic, substance-related, personality and neurodevelopmental disorders.

sections.heading: Causes, stigma, culture
sections.text: Most explanations use the biopsychosocial model: biological factors (genes, brain, physical illness), psychological factors (learning, appraisal, coping) and social factors (poverty, family stress, discrimination). The diathesis-stress model says a vulnerability may become disorder under stress. Stigma is a social process: public stigma, self-stigma and structural stigma (discrimination built into institutions and policies) can delay help. Culture shapes symptoms, idioms of distress (the ways a culture expresses suffering) and family responses. A behaviour that is normal in one setting may be pathological in another.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Case: Amina, a university student in Kano, has three weeks of low mood, poor sleep, guilt and cannot attend classes. A clinician checks duration, impairment and danger, rules out medical and substance causes, and uses ICD or DSM criteria plus her context. The formulation might include exam stress, family conflict and a family history of depression. Treatment could combine therapy, social support and, if indicated, medication. Confidentiality and local law apply.

keyPoints: No single criterion defines abnormality; distress, impairment and cultural context all matter.
ICD-11 is WHO’s system and DSM-5-TR is the American Psychiatric Association’s; editions and legal criteria vary, so check the current official source.
Reliability is agreement between clinicians; validity is whether a category captures a real condition.
The biopsychosocial model combines biological, psychological and social causes; diathesis-stress links vulnerability with stress.
Stigma can be public, self or structural and can delay help.
Culture shapes symptoms and idioms of distress, so assessment must be culturally informed.

en.title: Clinical Psychology: Assessment, Formulation and Intervention
en.short: Clinical assessment, case formulation, diagnosis, main interventions, teamwork and evidence limits.

sections.heading: Assessment and formulation
sections.text: Clinical assessment is the systematic gathering of information about a person’s difficulties, using interviews, observation, psychological tests, records and reports from others. Its aim is to describe problems, strengths, risk and context. Case formulation is a provisional explanation that links presenting problems to predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors. It guides what to assess next and what to try, and it is revised as evidence changes.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and case example
sections.text: Diagnosis assigns a label from a classification system. The DSM (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders), published by the American Psychiatric Association, and the ICD (International Classification of Diseases), published by the World Health Organization, are the main systems; editions and adoption vary by country, so check the current official version. A label can aid communication and access to care, but it does not explain a person’s case. For example, Amaka, a 24-year-old student in Enugu, presents with panic attacks before exams. Assessment rules out medical causes; formulation links perfectionism, sleep loss and avoidance. Diagnosis may be panic disorder, while formulation guides the intervention.

sections.heading: Main interventions
sections.text: Evidence-based psychological interventions include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which examines links between thoughts, feelings and behaviour; psychodynamic therapy, which explores recurring patterns and unconscious meaning; and systemic therapy, which works with relationships and family or community systems. Biomedical approaches use medication or other physical treatments. Medication is prescribed by a doctor, often a psychiatrist, and prescribing rights vary by country. For Amaka, CBT might include psychoeducation, breathing retraining and graded exposure to feared exam situations, with review of progress.

sections.heading: Boundaries and evidence
sections.text: Professional boundaries require working within training and competence, seeking supervision, obtaining informed consent and protecting confidentiality within its legal limits. Multidisciplinary work shares assessment and formulation across professions, with clear roles and coordination. Evidence has limits: trials often use selected samples and manualised treatments, where therapy follows a fixed written protocol, while real clients have comorbidity and cultural contexts. Publication bias and poor cultural validation matter. Evidence-based practice combines the best available research, clinical judgement and the person’s values and preferences.

keyPoints: Clinical assessment gathers information from several sources; case formulation explains why problems occur and guides treatment.
Diagnosis uses DSM or ICD and varies by country and edition; check the current official version.
CBT, psychodynamic and systemic therapies target different maintaining processes; biomedical treatment is prescribed by a doctor, often a psychiatrist.
Professional boundaries include competence, supervision, informed consent and confidentiality limits.
Multidisciplinary teams coordinate care but need clear roles and shared formulation.
Evidence-based practice uses research, clinical judgement and client values, while recognising limits of trials and cultural validity.

en.title: Counselling Psychology: Skills, Approaches and Ethics
en.short: Helping relationship, listening, empathy, questioning, main approaches, boundaries, referral and diversity.

sections.heading: Helping relationship and skills
sections.text: Counselling psychology studies how a trained helper uses a planned relationship to help a person explore difficulties and make changes. The helping relationship is the working alliance: agreed goals, tasks and emotional bond. Carl Rogers held that three conditions help: unconditional positive regard (acceptance without judgement), empathy (understanding and communicating the client’s frame of reference), and congruence (being genuine). Active listening means attending fully and showing understanding through posture, eye contact, minimal encouragers (brief prompts such as 'mm-hm'), paraphrasing and summarising. Paraphrasing restates content; reflecting feeling names emotion. Empathy is not sympathy: sympathy feels for the person from outside, empathy tries to feel with them. Open questions invite exploration, closed questions gather facts, and leading questions push an answer and should be avoided. Case: Amina, a student in Kano, says she cannot concentrate. The counsellor reflects, 'You feel overwhelmed since the exams moved closer.' Amina then clarifies her worry. That is active listening.

sections.heading: Comparing approaches
sections.text: Major approaches differ in focus. Person-centred therapy, from Rogers, trusts the client’s growth and lets the client lead. Psychodynamic counselling explores unconscious patterns, early relationships and transference, where feelings from past relationships enter the present. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) examines how thoughts and behaviours maintain distress and uses structured tasks. Systemic counselling treats problems as patterns in family interaction. Evidence and training vary by approach, and many counsellors integrate methods. No single approach suits every person or problem.

sections.heading: Boundaries and ethics
sections.text: Boundaries are limits on the relationship, such as time, confidentiality, touch and dual relationships (another tie with the client outside counselling, such as friend, teacher or business partner). Referral means passing a client to another professional when needs exceed competence or risk is high. Diversity requires attention to culture, language, religion, gender, disability and power. Ethical practice includes informed consent, confidentiality and its limits, supervision (regular review of the counsellor’s work with a senior colleague) and record keeping. Rules vary by country; check local law and the professional body. Case: the counsellor notices Amina’s risk of self-harm, keeps contact and refers her to a clinical service.

keyPoints: The helping relationship is a working alliance of goals, tasks and bond.
Rogers named unconditional positive regard, empathy and congruence as core conditions.
Active listening uses paraphrasing, reflecting feeling and open questions to show understanding.
Empathy tries to understand the client’s frame of reference; sympathy feels for the person from outside.
Person-centred, psychodynamic, cognitive behavioural and systemic approaches differ in focus and method.
Boundaries, referral, cultural awareness and ethical practice protect clients and counsellors.

en.title: Industrial and Organisational Psychology
en.short: Work psychology: motivation, satisfaction, selection, training, leadership, teams, culture, stress, ergonomics.

sections.heading: Motivation and satisfaction
sections.text:
Work motivation is the energising and directing of effort towards work goals. Job satisfaction is a person’s attitude to the job. Herzberg’s two-factor theory separates motivators such as achievement from hygiene factors such as pay; poor hygiene causes dissatisfaction, but good hygiene does not motivate.

Vroom’s expectancy theory says effort depends on expectancy (effort leads to performance), instrumentality (performance leads to rewards) and valence (how much the reward matters to the person), multiplied together. Equity theory says workers compare input-outcome ratios with others and reduce effort or leave if they feel under-rewarded. Goal-setting theory finds that specific, difficult goals with feedback raise performance.

sections.heading: Selection and training
sections.text:
Selection starts with job analysis, which describes tasks and the knowledge, skills and abilities needed. Good selection tools must be reliable and valid. Structured interviews and cognitive ability tests predict job performance better than unstructured interviews, but tests can create adverse impact, meaning unfair disadvantage for a group, so fairness must be checked.

Training begins with a needs analysis. Learning is helped by practice, feedback and similarity to the job, and transfer means using it at work. Kirkpatrick’s four levels evaluate reaction, learning, behaviour and results.

sections.heading: Performance, leadership, teams
sections.text:
Performance management is a cycle of setting goals, appraising against them, giving feedback and planning development. Leadership theory moved from traits to behaviours and then to contingency views: the best style depends on the situation. Transformational leaders inspire a shared vision; transactional leaders use rewards and monitoring.

In teams, roles, cohesion and coordination help, while social loafing is reduced by identifiable individual contributions. Organisational culture is the shared assumptions that guide behaviour; Schein describes artefacts, espoused values and basic assumptions.

sections.heading: Stress and ergonomics
sections.text:
Work stress arises when demands exceed a person’s resources. The demands-control-support model predicts strain when demands are high and control and support are low. Burnout is exhaustion, cynicism and reduced efficacy. Ergonomics fits the task, equipment and environment to human limits, covering posture, display design and mental workload.

Case: Ada, a Lagos call-centre supervisor, sees errors rise under long queues. She adds breaks, clearer targets and feedback; appraisal and training support the change.

keyPoints: Work motivation theories include Herzberg’s two-factor theory, Vroom’s expectancy theory (motivation = expectancy × instrumentality × valence), equity theory and goal-setting theory.
Job satisfaction is an attitude; selection tools must be reliable and valid and checked for adverse impact.
Training follows needs analysis and transfer; Kirkpatrick evaluates reaction, learning, behaviour and results.
Performance management links goals, appraisal, feedback and development; leadership style depends on the situation.
Teams need clear roles and coordination; culture is shared assumptions at artefact, value and basic-assumption levels.
Strain is highest when demands are high and control and support are low; ergonomics fits work to human limits.

en.title: Educational Psychology: Learning and Teaching in Classrooms
en.short: How psychology applies to classroom learning, motivation, expectations, assessment, inclusion and school culture.

sections.heading: Applying psychology
sections.text: Educational psychology applies psychological research to learning and teaching. It studies how pupils learn, what motivates them, how teachers assess progress and how schools respond to individual differences. It is an applied field, so findings are interpreted in context, not applied as fixed rules. Two useful ideas are scaffolding, temporary support such as worked steps or prompts that is reduced as competence grows, and the zone of proximal development, the gap between what a learner can do alone and with help. Teachers use these to set tasks that are challenging but achievable.

sections.heading: Motivation and assessment
sections.text: Motivation concerns why pupils engage and persist. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest or satisfaction; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or pressure. Clear goals, achievable challenge, feedback and belonging support motivation. Teacher expectations also matter. If teachers consistently treat some pupils as more capable, those pupils may get more attention and opportunity, and the expectation can become self-fulfilling. This is often called the Pygmalion effect, though effects vary. Assessment is gathering evidence about learning. Formative assessment happens during teaching and informs next steps; summative assessment summarises achievement at the end. Good assessment is valid (it measures intended learning) and reliable (it gives consistent results).

sections.heading: Differences and classroom
sections.text: Individual differences include prior knowledge, language, motivation, disability and learning difficulties. Differentiated instruction adjusts content, pace or support without lowering the goal. Special educational needs (SEN) require additional or different provision; inclusive education places pupils with SEN in ordinary classes with support where possible. Classroom management uses routines, clear expectations, active supervision and positive behaviour support. School culture is the shared norms and practices of a school, including how people treat one another. Case: in a secondary school in Ibadan, Mr Adeyemi finds pupils avoid fractions. He gives a short ungraded quiz, pairs pupils to explain steps and scaffolds examples. He uses the quiz to plan the next lesson.

keyPoints: Educational psychology applies research on learning, motivation, assessment and individual differences to classroom practice.
Scaffolding is temporary support that is reduced as a learner gains competence.
Teacher expectations can become self-fulfilling, but effects vary and should be checked.
Formative assessment informs teaching; summative assessment summarises achievement.
Differentiated instruction changes support or pace without lowering the learning goal.
Clear routines, positive behaviour support and a safe school culture support classroom learning.

en.title: Health Psychology: Stress, Health Behaviour and Chronic Illness
en.short: Stress, coping, health behaviour, adherence, pain, chronic illness, prevention and the biopsychosocial model.

sections.heading: Biopsychosocial model
sections.text:
Health psychology studies how biological, psychological and social factors together shape health, illness and care. The biopsychosocial model, proposed by George Engel, rejects a purely biomedical view. A person’s genes and physiology interact with beliefs, emotions, family, income, culture and health services.

Two people with the same infection may recover differently because one has social support and money for medicines. This model guides prevention and treatment.

sections.heading: Stress and coping
sections.text:
Stress is the response to demands appraised as exceeding a person’s resources. In Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model, primary appraisal judges whether an event is stressful, such as a threat or challenge, and secondary appraisal judges whether coping resources are enough. Coping is the effort to manage the demand.

Problem-focused coping changes the stressor; emotion-focused coping regulates distress; meaning-focused coping finds purpose. Social support can buffer stress. Family and community support are important in many settings, but poverty and stigma can weaken them. Long-term stress is linked with poorer physical and mental health.

sections.heading: Health behaviour and adherence
sections.text:
Health behaviours are actions that protect or harm health, such as diet, exercise, condom use, vaccination and smoking. The health belief model says uptake depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers and cues to action. The stages of change model describes movement from precontemplation to maintenance.

Adherence means following an agreed treatment plan. It is affected by regimen complexity, side effects, cost, beliefs, stigma and clinician communication. Case: Amina in Kano stops her asthma preventer because she feels well and the clinic is far. A nurse discusses cost and sets a phone reminder.

sections.heading: Pain, chronic illness, prevention
sections.text:
Pain is subjective, shaped by tissue damage, attention, emotion and culture. Gate control theory says spinal signals can be modulated, so anxiety may increase pain and distraction may reduce it. Chronic illness needs long-term self-management.

Prevention has three levels: primary stops disease before onset, secondary detects it early, tertiary limits disability. Health promotion helps people gain control over health through education, policy and supportive environments. Culture, poverty and stigma shape symptoms and care.

keyPoints: The biopsychosocial model explains health through biological, psychological and social factors together.
Stress depends on appraisal of demands and resources, and coping may target the problem or the distress.
The health belief model and stages of change model explain how health behaviours start and are maintained.
Adherence is following an agreed treatment plan and is shaped by cost, side effects, beliefs and communication.
Pain is subjective and can be modulated by attention, emotion and culture.
Prevention is primary, secondary or tertiary, and health promotion creates supportive conditions for health.

en.title: Psychometrics and Psychological Testing
en.short: Test construction, item analysis, reliability, validity, norms, fairness and ethical use of psychological tests.

sections.heading: Construction and items
sections.text: Psychometrics is the science of measuring psychological attributes. Construction starts with a clear definition of the construct and a table of specifications linking items to content. Items are tried out on a sample. Item difficulty p is the proportion answering correctly. Item discrimination shows whether an item separates stronger from weaker candidates; a simple index is D = p(upper group) − p(lower group), using the top and bottom 27 per cent. Example: if 5 of 5 in the upper group and 2 of 5 in the lower group answer correctly, p = 1.00 and 0.40, so D = 0.60. Items that are very easy, very hard or have low D are revised or dropped.

sections.heading: Reliability and validity
sections.text: Reliability is consistency of scores. Test-retest reliability repeats the test after a gap; alternate-form reliability uses two versions; internal consistency (split-half, Cronbach’s alpha) checks how closely the items hang together; inter-rater reliability checks agreement between scorers. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Validity is evidence that scores support the intended interpretation. Content validity covers the construct’s domain; construct validity is the overall network of evidence; criterion validity compares scores with an outcome, concurrently or predictively. Face validity is only surface plausibility. A test can be reliable but invalid, like a scale that consistently measures the wrong thing.

sections.heading: Norms, fairness and ethics
sections.text: Standardisation means fixed administration and scoring, plus norms from a representative group. Scores may be reported as percentiles, z scores (mean 0, SD 1) or T scores (mean 50, SD 10). A norm is not a universal standard: it belongs to its population and date. Fairness requires evidence that items function similarly across groups, called differential item functioning, and that language and culture suit the test-taker. Intelligence tests estimate general cognitive ability; aptitude tests predict learning in a specific area; achievement tests measure what has been taught; personality tests describe typical traits, usually by self-report. Ethical use requires consent, confidentiality, competence, secure materials, feedback and awareness of local law.

keyPoints: Item difficulty is p = number correct ÷ number tested; discrimination D = p(upper) − p(lower).
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether scores support the intended interpretation.
Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.
Standardisation fixes administration and scoring and provides norms from a representative group.
Fairness needs evidence of differential item functioning and suitable language and culture.
Ethical testing requires consent, confidentiality, competence and feedback; rules vary by country.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods in Psychology
en.short: Advanced design, sampling, measurement, validity, ethics and reporting in psychology research.

sections.heading: Design and measurement
sections.text:
Advanced work starts by matching the question to a design. Experiments manipulate an independent variable and randomise participants, which supports causal claims. Factorial designs test two or more factors and their interaction, the effect of one factor depending on another. Quasi-experiments lack random assignment but can still support causal inference, for example through regression discontinuity or interrupted time series. Correlational designs measure variables as they are and cannot establish causation. Qualitative research, including thematic analysis and ethnography, studies meaning and context in depth.

Measurement must be reliable, meaning consistent, and valid, meaning it measures the intended construct. Measurement invariance means a scale carries the same meaning across groups; without it, group comparisons may mislead.

sections.heading: Sampling and validity
sections.text:
Probability sampling, such as simple random or stratified sampling, lets every member of the population have a known chance of selection. Non-probability samples, such as convenience samples, are common in psychology but limit generalisation. Estimate the sample size needed before data collection, and plan for attrition.

Validity threats include internal threats (history, maturation, attrition), external threats (narrow samples), construct threats (poor measures) and statistical conclusion threats (low power, multiple testing). A small case: Ada tests a study-skills workshop in a Nigerian secondary school. She randomises 60 students, 30 to the workshop and 30 to a wait-list. After dropout, 27 and 29 remain. She plans an intention-to-treat analysis, keeping all randomised students in their assigned groups, to protect the randomisation.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text:
Research ethics requires informed consent, confidentiality, protection of vulnerable participants, and approval from an ethics committee.

Analysis planning means stating hypotheses, outcomes and tests before data collection, often through pre-registration. This reduces researcher degrees of freedom, the many choices that can inflate false positives. Report methods and results transparently, following guidelines such as CONSORT for trials and PRISMA for reviews, and make data and materials available where possible.

keyPoints: Experiments with random assignment support causal claims; correlational designs do not.
Factorial designs test main effects and interactions.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; convenience sampling limits it.
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether a measure captures the intended construct.
Pre-registration and an analysis plan limit researcher degrees of freedom.
Ethics approval, informed consent and transparent reporting are required.

en.title: Ethics and Professional Practice in Psychology
en.short: Informed consent, confidentiality, competence, boundaries, research ethics and ethical decisions.

sections.heading: Core duties
sections.text: Professional ethics sets standards for what psychologists owe clients, participants and the public. Informed consent means giving enough information, checking understanding and obtaining voluntary agreement before assessment, therapy or research. It can be withdrawn. Confidentiality means not disclosing private information without permission. Its limits depend on the country and profession, and may include serious risk of harm, child protection, court orders or supervision. Competence means practising only within training and experience, keeping skills current, and referring when needed. Psychologists also have duties of integrity, respect and care, often summarised as beneficence (helping), nonmaleficence (doing no harm), justice (fairness) and fidelity (keeping trust). Codes and laws vary by country and professional body, so practitioners must check the current local code and statute.

sections.heading: Boundaries and research
sections.text: Boundaries are the limits that define the professional relationship. A dual or multiple relationship exists when a psychologist has another significant role with a client, such as teacher, employer, relative or friend. Not all are harmful, but they can impair judgement or exploit power, so they need scrutiny and usually avoidance. Research ethics requires voluntary informed consent, privacy, anonymity or confidentiality, minimising harm, honest reporting and ethics review. Deception is used only when justified and must be explained in debriefing, where participants are told the truth afterwards. Vulnerable groups need extra safeguards.

sections.heading: Ethical decisions
sections.text: Ethical decision making is a structured process: identify the dilemma and facts; consult the code, law and colleagues; consider affected parties and cultural context; list options and consequences; act; document; review. Responsibilities include protecting welfare, maintaining records, managing conflicts of interest and speaking up about unethical practice.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: A psychologist in Lagos, Nigeria counsels a university student, Tunde. Tunde’s lecturer asks for his counselling notes. The psychologist does not release them without Tunde’s consent or a lawful order. If Tunde disclosed imminent danger to himself or another person, the psychologist would follow local law and code, seek consultation and disclose only what is necessary. The psychologist also avoids becoming Tunde’s lecturer or business partner, because that dual relationship could harm the therapy.

keyPoints: Informed consent requires information, understanding and voluntary agreement, and it can be withdrawn.
Confidentiality has legal and ethical limits that vary by country and must be explained to clients.
Competence means working within training and experience and referring when necessary.
Dual relationships can impair judgement or exploit power, so they require scrutiny and usually avoidance.
Research ethics requires consent, privacy, minimising harm, honest reporting and ethics review.
Ethical decisions should be structured, documented and reviewed, using the local code and law.

en.title: Cross-Cultural and African Psychology
en.short: Culture in psychology, universality, measurement equivalence, indigenisation and African-centred debates.

sections.heading: Culture and psychology
sections.text: Culture is the shared, learned and changing set of meanings, practices and values through which people interpret life. Cross-cultural psychology compares psychological processes across societies. Cultural psychology studies how local meanings shape those processes. Both reject the idea that one country’s sample, usually a Western one, can stand for all people. But culture is not a single trait.
