Within any country there are regional, religious, class, gender and generational differences, so “Nigerian culture” or “African culture” is shorthand, not a uniform thing.

sections.heading: Universality and specificity
sections.text: Universality means a process works in the same way everywhere. Cultural specificity means its meaning, expression or development depends on context. Basic perception and learning may show broad regularities, while emotion display, self-description and family obligation vary. The etic approach uses categories from outside a culture; the emic approach starts with insiders’ own terms. Good research combines them. A claim of universality is not proved by testing one group and assuming the rest.

sections.heading: Measurement equivalence
sections.text: Measurement equivalence asks whether a test measures the same construct in each group. Construct equivalence means the items carry the same meaning. Metric equivalence means score units are comparable. Scalar equivalence means full scores can be compared. Without these, a mean difference may come from translation, response style or unfamiliar items, not culture. A Lagos researcher translating a depression scale into Yoruba, for example, must check idioms and back-translation, then test invariance before comparing students in Lagos and London.

sections.heading: Indigenisation and African debates
sections.text: Indigenisation adapts psychology to local languages, problems and meanings rather than importing theories unchanged. African-centred perspectives include African psychology, Afrocentric and community-oriented approaches. They emphasise collective selfhood, spirituality, oral knowledge and colonial history, but they are not one voice. Decolonising psychology asks whose categories, agendas and languages dominate, and who benefits. Some argue for reforming mainstream psychology; others for building separate traditions. In practice, a Ghanaian counselling service might combine local family and religious support with standard assessment, while checking that neither approach treats clients as stereotypes.

keyPoints: Culture is shared and learned but not uniform within a group.
Universality claims need evidence from more than one cultural context.
Etic categories come from outside; emic categories come from inside a culture.
Measurement equivalence must be checked before comparing group means.
Indigenisation adapts psychology to local meanings, languages and problems.
Decolonising psychology is debated as reform, replacement or both.

en.title: The Psychology Research Project: From Question to Report
en.short: From research question and literature review to ethics, data, analysis, writing and presentation.

sections.heading: From question to plan
sections.text:
A final-year project starts with a question that is narrow, answerable and ethical. Read the literature to find what is known and where a gap remains. Turn each concept into an operational definition, meaning the exact way you will measure it. Choose a design and a sample you can actually reach.

Write a short plan: question, hypotheses, method, analysis and timetable. In a case, Amina in Kano studies sleep and exam stress. She defines stress as a score on a validated scale and sleep as average hours per night, then checks that her department can approve the study in time.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Before collecting data, submit the protocol to your department’s ethics committee or institutional review board (IRB). Explain the purpose, risks, consent, confidentiality and data storage. Informed consent means participants freely agree after understanding what will happen. Keep data secure and anonymise it where possible.

Collect data exactly as approved and record any problems. Do not change questions midway without approval.

sections.heading: Analysis and interpretation
sections.text:
Follow the analysis plan, but say clearly if you add exploratory tests. Check assumptions and report effect sizes with confidence intervals, not only p values. Interpret results against your question and the literature. A non-significant result is still a result.

Limitations are the boundaries of what you can claim: a small sample, self-report bias, or one setting. State them plainly and do not overgeneralise.

sections.heading: Writing and presenting
sections.text:
Use a clear scientific structure: introduction, method, results, discussion and references. Write plainly, define abbreviations, report numbers consistently and cite sources accurately. Avoid plagiarism and agree authorship early. In the discussion, separate findings from speculation.

In the presentation, state the question, method, main result and limitation in that order. Keep slides simple and answer questions honestly. Responsible reporting means reporting all planned outcomes, not hiding inconvenient data, and keeping data available for checking.

keyPoints: A research question should be narrow, answerable and ethical.
Operational definitions state exactly how variables are measured.
Ethics approval and informed consent come before data collection.
Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p values.
Limitations define the boundaries of your claims.
Responsible reporting means reporting all planned outcomes and keeping data available.

en.title: Advanced Cognitive Neuroscience
en.short: Methods, neural systems and models for attention, memory, language and executive control.

sections.heading: Systems and control
sections.text: Advanced cognitive neuroscience links mental functions to brain systems. Attention is supported by frontoparietal networks that bias processing toward relevant stimuli; alerting, orienting and executive attention can be studied separately. Memory depends on medial temporal lobe structures, especially the hippocampus, plus prefrontal and posterior cortex. Language relies on a left-hemisphere perisylvian network. Executive control means processes that regulate thought and action: working memory updating, inhibition, task switching and conflict monitoring, linked to prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex. Systems interact, so tasks rarely isolate one function.

sections.heading: Methods and inference
sections.text: Methods differ in what they can infer. EEG (electroencephalography) records scalp electrical activity with millisecond temporal resolution but poor spatial localisation. fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging) measures the BOLD signal, a blood-oxygen proxy for neural activity, with good spatial but slow temporal resolution. Lesion studies test necessity: damage that impairs a function implicates the region, though plasticity complicates inference. Brain stimulation, such as TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation) or tDCS (transcranial direct current stimulation), perturbs a region and observes the effect, giving reversible causal evidence. Convergent evidence is stronger than one result.

sections.heading: Computational models
sections.text: Computational models make mechanisms explicit and testable. A drift-diffusion model treats a decision as noisy evidence accumulation from a starting point to a threshold. Drift rate indexes evidence quality, boundary separation indexes caution, and non-decision time covers encoding and motor output. Fitting the model to response times and accuracy can separate processes that raw scores confound. Models are judged by prediction and comparison, not realism alone.

sections.heading: Critical appraisal
sections.text: Critical appraisal asks whether a result supports the claimed mental process. A study may report stronger left prefrontal fMRI signal during a working-memory task. That does not prove the region stores items, because the task also demands attention, strategy and response preparation. This is the reverse inference problem. Checks include task impurity, multiple comparisons, double dipping, small samples and publication bias. Stronger designs combine methods, preregister predictions and report effect sizes. Replication across methods is the best safeguard.

keyPoints: Cognitive neuroscience combines brain measures with cognitive tasks to test how mental functions are implemented.
EEG has high temporal but low spatial resolution; fMRI has high spatial but low temporal resolution.
Lesion and brain stimulation studies can support causal claims, but plasticity and task differences limit inference.
Reverse inference is the mistake of treating a brain activation as proof of a specific mental process.
Computational models such as drift-diffusion separate latent processes and must be compared against alternatives.
Convergent evidence from several methods is stronger than any single study.

en.title: Advanced Social Psychology: Theory, Replication and Application
en.short: Covers advanced social cognition, attitudes, intergroup relations, culture, relationships, replication and application.

sections.heading: Social cognition and attitudes
sections.text: Advanced social psychology studies how people perceive, interpret and act on social information. Social cognition covers schemas (mental templates), heuristics (quick rules), attribution (explaining behaviour) and automatic versus controlled processing. Attitudes are evaluations of objects, people or issues. Explicit measures ask directly; implicit measures infer associations. Attitudes predict behaviour better when they are specific, accessible and supported by norms and perceived control. Research design must separate measurement from manipulation and check reliability and validity.

sections.heading: Intergroup relations and culture
sections.text: Intergroup theory asks how group membership shapes identity and conflict. Social identity theory holds that people derive self-esteem from ingroups and may favour them. Contact theory predicts that positive contact under cooperation, equal status and institutional support can reduce prejudice. Culture shapes self-construal: independent versus interdependent selves, and affects attribution, emotion and relationship norms. Samples are often from Western, educated, industrialised settings, so claims need testing elsewhere.

sections.heading: Relationships and replication
sections.text: Relationship research examines attachment, interdependence and social exchange. Advanced designs use longitudinal data, dyadic models (analyses of pairs of people, such as couples) and moderation and mediation tests. Replication is central: large multi-team studies show that many social effects are smaller than first reported. Pre-registration, open data, adequate power and direct replication improve credibility. A case: a team tests a contact intervention among Lagos university students, randomises workshops, measures prejudice before and after, pre-registers the analysis and repeats it on another campus. Null or weak results are still informative.

sections.heading: Applied implications
sections.text: Applied social psychology uses these findings in health, education, organisations and policy. Interventions should be theory-based, ethically approved and evaluated with control groups. Effects found in one culture or setting may not transfer. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only significance.

keyPoints: Social cognition includes schemas, heuristics, attribution and automatic versus controlled processing.
Attitudes are evaluations; explicit and implicit measures tap different aspects and predict behaviour under different conditions.
Social identity theory and contact theory explain ingroup favouritism and prejudice reduction.
Culture shapes self-construal, attribution and relationship norms, so findings need testing across settings.
Replication, pre-registration, adequate power and open data are central to credible advanced social psychology.
Applied interventions need theory, ethical approval and controlled evaluation before scale-up.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Statistics
en.short: Multivariate models, SEM, multilevel data, meta-analysis, qualitative methods and open science.

sections.heading: Regression and ANOVA
sections.text:
Regression models an outcome as a weighted sum of predictors; each coefficient is the expected change in the outcome for a one-unit rise in that predictor, holding others fixed. R² is the proportion of variance explained. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compares group means using F = MS_between ÷ MS_within; factorial ANOVA adds interaction tests. Multivariate methods handle several outcomes or predictors at once.

Worked example: if y = 40 + 5x and x = 6, predicted y = 70. An observed y of 68 gives residual −2. This is association under assumptions, not proof of cause.

sections.heading: SEM, multilevel and meta-analysis
sections.text:
Structural equation modelling (SEM) joins a measurement model, linking indicators to latent variables, with a structural model of paths among them, so a whole theory is tested. Multilevel models handle nested data, such as students within schools, splitting variance into between-group and within-group parts: ICC = σ²_between ÷ (σ²_between + σ²_within). If between variance is 4 and within variance is 16, ICC = 4 ÷ 20 = 0.20.

Meta-analysis pools effect sizes, often weighting by inverse variance: pooled θ = Σw_iθ_i ÷ Σw_i. Heterogeneity statistics such as I² show variation beyond sampling error.

sections.heading: Qualitative and open science
sections.text:
Qualitative methods, such as interviews and thematic analysis, study meaning and context. They use purposive sampling, coding and reflexivity, and are judged by credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability rather than p-values.

Open science means transparent practice: preregistration, open data and code, and registered reports. Reproducibility is getting the same results from the same data and analysis; replicability is similar results in a new study. Publication bias and p-hacking (trying analyses until something is significant) distort evidence. Responsible interpretation reports effect sizes and confidence intervals, checks assumptions, and does not treat statistical significance as proof.

keyPoints: Regression coefficients give the change in the outcome per one-unit rise in a predictor, holding others fixed.
ANOVA compares group means with F = MS_between ÷ MS_within.
SEM combines a measurement model of latent variables with a structural model of paths.
ICC = σ²_between ÷ (σ²_between + σ²_within) measures how much variance lies between groups.
Meta-analysis pools effect sizes, often as pooled θ = Σw_iθ_i ÷ Σw_i, and reports heterogeneity.
Open science, reproducibility and honest reporting of effect sizes protect against distorted evidence.

en.title: Research Design and the Master’s Dissertation
en.short: Covers planning, ethics, data, analysis, writing, supervision and defence of a master’s dissertation.

sections.heading: Shaping the question
sections.text: A master’s dissertation is an examined piece of independent research. It begins with an advanced research question: a focused, answerable question that existing work has not settled. A good question is feasible with your time, skills and access, and it matters to theory or practice. The literature review is not a list of summaries. It maps what is known, compares findings, and identifies the gap your study addresses. It also justifies your design. In a case, Amina in Nairobi asks whether a brief breathing exercise lowers test anxiety among first-year students. Her review shows small prior studies with mixed results, so her question targets that uncertainty.

sections.heading: Proposal and ethics
sections.text: Write a proposal that states the question, aims, design, participants, measures, analysis plan, timeline and limits. Ethical approval comes before data collection. A committee checks informed consent, confidentiality, risk and vulnerable groups. Rules differ by country and institution, so check your current requirements. A data management plan says how data will be collected, stored, accessed, anonymised and kept. It protects participants and makes analysis auditable.

sections.heading: Analysis and interpretation
sections.text: Analysis must fit the question and design. Descriptive summaries come first, then the planned inferential test or qualitative coding. Interpretation separates what the data show from what you hoped. Report effect sizes, uncertainty and limitations where relevant. Do not claim causation from a design that cannot support it. Scientific writing is plain, structured and evidence led: each claim is supported, and methods are reported clearly enough to repeat. Follow your department’s style guide.

sections.heading: Supervision and defence
sections.text: Supervision is a working relationship, not a substitute for your judgement. Agree regular meetings, send written drafts, and act on feedback. The thesis is often examined by internal and external examiners, and many programmes include an oral defence or viva. Procedures vary by country and university. Prepare by knowing your question, method, main finding and limits. In the defence, answer precisely and accept limits honestly.

keyPoints: A dissertation answers a focused, feasible and worthwhile research question.
The literature review identifies the gap and justifies the design, not just summarises sources.
Ethical approval is required before data collection; many institutions also require a data management plan, and rules vary by country and institution.
Analysis must match the question and design, and interpretation must separate findings from speculation.
Supervision works best with regular meetings, written drafts and honest response to feedback.
Examiners judge the thesis, and an oral defence or viva is common but procedures vary by country and university.
